90602.m: Unripe blackberries are green at first and then red.

90603.e: Blackberries ripen in late summer. You can often find them until well into autumn.
90603.m: Blackberries are picked in late summer.

90604.q: Which berry is the blackberry closely related to?
90604.e: The blackberry and the raspberry belong to the same plant genus. Both have fruits made of lots of little balls.
90604.m: The blackberry is related to the raspberry.

90605.q: What is a single blackberry made of?
90605.e: A blackberry is an aggregate fruit. Each little ball contains a tiny pip.
90605.m: A blackberry is made of lots of little balls.

a: As a mushroom on the ground
90606.e: Blackberries form long, prickly shoots. They quickly grow into a dense tangle.

90607.q: What colour are the flowers of the bramble?
90607.e: The bramble flowers white or pale pink in summer. The berries grow from the flowers.
90607.m: The bramble flowers white to pink.

90608.q: Which part of the bramble is often used to make tea?
90608.e: Young bramble leaves are dried. A mild tea is made from them.
90608.m: Tea is made from bramble leaves.

90609.q: Which forest animal likes to eat bramble leaves in winter?
90609.e: Bramble leaves often stay green into the winter. Roe deer find food in them when little else is growing.
90609.m: Roe deer like to eat bramble leaves in winter.

90610.q: What colour are the berries of privet?
90610.e: In autumn privet has shiny black berries. They often hang on into the winter.

90611.e: Privet berries are poisonous for people. You should never eat them.

90612.q: What colour are the flowers of privet?
90612.e: Privet flowers in early summer with small white flowers. They grow together in clusters.

90613.q: What do privet flowers smell like?
90613.e: The flowers have a strong, sweetish scent. It attracts lots of insects.
90613.m: Privet flowers have a strong scent.

90614.q: What is privet often planted for in gardens?
90614.e: Privet copes very well with being cut. That is why it is a popular hedge plant.
90614.m: Privet is a popular garden hedge.

90615.q: What happens to many privet leaves in winter?
a: They stay green for a long time
They fall off as early as July
90615.e: Privet often keeps its leaves well into the winter. In mild winters it stays almost completely green.
90615.m: Privet often stays green for a long time in winter.

90616.q: A big green caterpillar likes to eat privet leaves. What does it turn into later?
90616.e: The caterpillar of the privet hawk-moth eats privet leaves. Later it becomes a pupa, and a big moth hatches from it.
90616.m: The caterpillar turns into a moth.

90617.q: Who eats privet berries in winter?
90617.e: The berries are poisonous for people. But thrushes and other birds eat them in winter.
90617.m: Birds eat privet berries in winter.

90618.q: What colour are the fruits of the spindle tree?
90618.e: In autumn the fruits of the spindle tree glow pink to purplish red. You can see them from far away.
90618.m: The fruits of the spindle tree are pink.

90619.q: What colour is the covering around the seeds of the spindle tree?
90619.e: When the fruit splits open, you can see the seeds. They sit inside an orange coat.
90619.m: The seeds of the spindle tree have an orange coat.

90620.q: What is true of the fruits of the spindle tree?
90620.e: All parts of the spindle tree are poisonous, especially the seeds. You must never eat the colourful fruits.
90620.m: The spindle tree is very poisonous.

90621.q: In German the spindle tree is called “priest's little hat”. What does the shape of its fruit remind people of?
90621.e: The fruit looks like an old kind of cap worn by Catholic priests. In the past priests were also called “Pfaffen” in German.
90621.m: The fruit of the spindle tree looks like a priest's cap.

90622.q: Who likes to eat the seeds of the spindle tree without getting ill?
90622.e: The spindle tree is poisonous for people and many animals. But birds such as the robin like to eat the seeds. That is why it is also called robin's bread in German.
90622.m: Birds eat the seeds of the spindle tree.

90623.q: What kind of plant is the spindle tree?
90623.e: The spindle tree is a shrub. It often grows at the edges of woods and in hedges.
90623.m: The spindle tree is a shrub.

90624.q: What colour do many leaves of the spindle tree turn in autumn?
90624.e: In autumn many leaves turn bright red. Together with the fruits, the shrub is very colourful.
90624.m: The spindle tree has red leaves in autumn.

90625.q: What was the wood of the spindle tree used for in the past?
90625.e: The hard, fine wood was good for making hand spindles. That is why the shrub is called the spindle tree.
90625.m: Spindles were made from spindle wood.

90626.q: What colour are the flowers of the cornelian cherry?
90626.e: The cornelian cherry has golden yellow flowers. The small flowers grow in clusters on the bare twigs.

90627.q: When does the cornelian cherry flower?
a: As early as February and March
90627.e: The cornelian cherry is one of the first shrubs to flower. The flowers come before the leaves.
90627.m: The cornelian cherry flowers very early in the year.

90628.q: What colour are the ripe fruits of the cornelian cherry?
90628.e: The fruits are oval and shiny red. They look a little like small cherries.
90628.m: The fruits of the cornelian cherry are red.

90629.q: Can you eat the fruits of the cornelian cherry?
90629.e: The fruits are edible and taste sourish. When fully ripe they are sweeter, and people make jam from them.
90629.m: The fruits of the cornelian cherry are edible.

90630.q: What else is the cornelian cherry called in German-speaking Switzerland?
90630.e: In German-speaking Switzerland the cornelian cherry is also called Tierlibaum. In Austria it is called Dirndlstrauch.
90630.m: In Switzerland the cornelian cherry is also called Tierlibaum.

90631.q: What is the wood of the cornelian cherry like?
90631.e: The wood of the cornelian cherry is very hard and heavy. It is hard to split.
90631.m: The cornelian cherry has very hard wood.

90632.q: Why is the cornelian cherry important for bees?
a: It flowers when there is still little food
It has water in its flowers
It builds honeycombs for the bees
90632.e: In early spring hardly anything is flowering yet. The cornelian cherry is then one of the first food plants for bees.
90632.m: The cornelian cherry is bee food early in the year.

90633.q: Is the cornelian cherry a real cherry?
a: No, its fruits only look similar
Yes, it is a sour cherry
Yes, it is a wild sweet cherry
Yes, it is a small dwarf cherry
90633.e: The cornelian cherry is not a real cherry. Its red fruits only look a bit like cherries.
90633.m: The cornelian cherry is not a real cherry.

90634.q: What colour are the twigs of the common dogwood often in winter?
90634.e: In winter, when there are no leaves, the twigs often glow red. They are especially bright on the sunny side.
90634.m: The common dogwood has red twigs in winter.

90635.q: What colour are the flowers of the common dogwood?
90635.e: The common dogwood flowers in early summer. Lots of small white flowers grow in flat clusters.

90636.q: What colour are the fruits of the common dogwood?
90636.e: In autumn the shrub has small, bluish black fruits. Birds like to eat them.
90636.m: The fruits of the common dogwood are bluish black.

90637.q: Should you eat the fruits of the common dogwood raw?
90637.e: The raw fruits taste bitter and do not agree with people. It is better to leave them for the birds.
90637.m: You do not eat the fruits of the common dogwood raw.

90638.q: What do you see if you carefully pull a leaf of the common dogwood apart?
90638.e: When you pull it apart, the two halves of the leaf stay joined by fine white threads. This is a good way to recognise dogwood.
90638.m: Dogwood leaves have fine threads in their veins.

90639.q: The German name of the dogwood, “Hartriegel”, contains the word for “hard”. What does it refer to?
90639.e: The shrub has very hard wood. In the past, tool handles, for example, were made from it.

90640.q: How do the veins run on a leaf of the common dogwood?
a: In curves towards the tip of the leaf
Like a star from the stalk
Not at all, it has none
90640.e: The side veins curve forward towards the tip of the leaf. This is a good way to recognise it.

90641.q: Where does the common dogwood like to grow?
a: At the edges of woods and in hedges
In the middle of the water
90641.e: The common dogwood is a common shrub at the edges of woods and in hedges. It likes sun and partial shade.
90641.m: The common dogwood likes to grow in hedges.

90642.q: What does the hedgehog have on its back?
90642.e: The hedgehog's back is covered with sharp spines. They protect it from enemies.
90642.m: The hedgehog has spines on its back.

90643.q: About how many spines does an adult hedgehog have?
90643.e: An adult hedgehog has about 6,000 to 8,000 spines. They are hollow and light.

90644.q: When is the hedgehog mainly out and about?
a: Only in the rain during the day
90644.e: The hedgehog is a nocturnal animal. During the day it sleeps hidden in leaves or in the hedge.
90644.m: The hedgehog looks for food at night.

90645.q: What does a hedgehog mainly eat?
90645.e: The hedgehog eats beetles, caterpillars, earthworms and slugs. It finds them with its good nose.
90645.m: The hedgehog eats beetles and worms.

90646.q: Where does a hedgehog often sleep through the winter?
90646.e: The hedgehog builds its winter nest from dry leaves and grass. It is often under a hedge or a pile of branches.
90646.m: The hedgehog spends the winter in a nest of leaves.

90647.q: Why is a hedge good for the hedgehog?
90647.e: The hedgehog can hide in the hedge. Lots of beetles and worms also live under the shrubs.
90647.m: The hedgehog finds shelter and food in the hedge.

90648.e: The red-backed shrike is a songbird, a bit bigger than a sparrow. It likes to live in thorny hedges.
90648.m: The red-backed shrike is a bird.

90649.q: What does the red-backed shrike do with its prey?
a: It buries it in the ground
It hides it in the water
It puts it in its nest under leaves
90649.e: The red-backed shrike spikes insects and other prey on thorns. In the past people believed it caught nine animals first, which is why its German name means nine-killer. In English shrikes are also called butcher birds.
90649.m: The red-backed shrike spikes its prey on thorns.

90650.q: Why does the red-backed shrike spike its prey?
a: It makes a store of food
It dries it for the nest
90650.e: In bad weather there are few insects. Then the shrike eats from its spiked stores.
90650.m: The red-backed shrike makes food stores.

90651.q: What does the male red-backed shrike have on its face?
90651.e: The male has a black stripe across its eyes. It looks like a mask.
90651.m: The male red-backed shrike has a black mask.

90652.q: Where does the red-backed shrike spend the winter?
90652.e: The red-backed shrike is a migrating bird. In autumn it flies all the way to southern Africa.
90652.m: The red-backed shrike spends the winter in Africa.

90653.q: When does the red-backed shrike come back to us in spring?
90653.e: The red-backed shrike comes back late, usually at the beginning of May. By then there are enough big insects.
90653.m: The red-backed shrike comes back in May.

90654.q: What does the red-backed shrike mainly eat?
90654.e: It mainly hunts beetles, bumblebees and grasshoppers. Sometimes it also catches a mouse.
90654.m: The red-backed shrike mainly eats big insects.

90655.q: Where does the red-backed shrike build its nest?
a: In the reeds by the water
90655.e: It likes to build its nest in blackthorn, roses or brambles. The thorns protect the young.
90655.m: The red-backed shrike nests in thorny shrubs.

90656.q: Roughly how much of the Earth's surface is covered by sea?
90656.e: Around 71 per cent of the Earth is covered by sea. That is why the Earth is also called the blue planet.
90656.m: More than two thirds of the Earth is sea.

90657.q: What in the sea produces about half the oxygen we breathe?
90657.e: Tiny algae in the sea make oxygen just like plants. They are called phytoplankton.
90657.m: Tiny algae in the sea make a lot of oxygen.

90658.q: What is it like in the deep sea?
90658.e: Sunlight does not reach down into the deep sea. The water there is only a few degrees warm.
90658.m: The deep sea is dark and cold.

90659.q: What is the deepest place in the oceans called?
90659.e: The Mariana Trench lies in the Pacific. That is where the sea is deepest.
90659.m: The Mariana Trench is the deepest place in the sea.

90660.q: Roughly how deep is the Mariana Trench?
90660.e: At its deepest point, the trench is almost 11,000 metres deep. That is about 11 kilometres.
90660.m: The Mariana Trench is about 11 kilometres deep.

90661.q: What are hot springs on the deep seabed that pour out dark water called?
90661.e: On the seabed there are springs that pour out very hot, dark water. They are called black smokers, and special animals live around them.
90661.m: Black smokers are hot springs in the deep sea.

90662.q: What is especially great in the deep sea?
90662.e: There is a huge amount of water above the deep sea. It presses with enormous force on everything down there.
90662.m: In the deep sea, the water presses very hard.

90663.q: Which Swiss man was one of the first to dive to the deepest point in the sea in 1960?
90663.e: In 1960 Jacques Piccard dived into the Mariana Trench with the American Don Walsh. No one had ever managed that before.
90663.m: Jacques Piccard dived into the Mariana Trench in 1960.

90664.q: Do we already know all the animals of the deep sea?
a: Yes, there are no animals there
90664.e: The deep sea is hard to explore. Researchers keep discovering new animal species there.
90664.m: There are still many unknown animals in the deep sea.

90665.q: Which large whale dives very deep to hunt squid?
90665.e: The sperm whale dives more than 1000 metres deep. There it hunts squid.
90665.m: The sperm whale hunts squid in the deep sea.

90666.q: Where is the largest coral reef in the world?
90666.e: The Great Barrier Reef lies off the coast of Australia. It is so big that it can be seen from space.
90666.m: The largest coral reef is off Australia.

90667.q: In which water do coral reefs grow best?
90667.e: Reef corals need warm, clear and fairly shallow sea water. That is why they are found mainly in the tropics.
90667.m: Coral reefs grow in warm seas.

90668.q: What happens to corals when the sea gets too warm?
90668.e: When the water is too warm, corals lose their colourful algae. Then they turn white, which is called coral bleaching.
90668.m: Water that is too warm makes corals bleach.

90669.q: Which orange and white fish lives in the reef among sea anemones?
90669.e: The clownfish lives among the tentacles of sea anemones. A layer of slime protects it from their stings.
90669.m: The clownfish lives in sea anemones.

90670.q: How fast does a coral reef grow?
90670.e: Many corals grow only a few millimetres to centimetres a year. A large reef takes thousands of years.

90671.q: What lives inside corals and helps feed them?
90671.e: Tiny algae live inside the corals. They make food from sunlight and give the corals their colours.
90671.m: Tiny algae help feed the corals.

90672.q: Why are coral reefs also called the rainforests of the sea?
a: A great many animal species live there
90672.e: A great many different animals live in coral reefs. That is similar to the rainforest on land.
90672.m: A great many animal species live in a coral reef.

90673.e: A submarine is a boat that travels under the sea. It can dive and move along underwater.

90674.q: What does a submarine let into its tanks in order to dive?
90674.e: When water flows into the tanks, the submarine becomes heavier. Then it sinks down.
90674.m: With water in its tanks, the submarine dives.

90675.q: How does a submarine get back to the surface?
a: Air pushes the water out of the tanks
It waits for a big wave
A ship pulls it up on a rope
90675.e: Compressed air pushes the water out of the tanks. The submarine becomes lighter and rises.
90675.m: Air in the tanks makes the submarine rise.

90676.q: What do you use to look above the water from a submerged submarine?
90676.e: A periscope sticks out of the water and uses mirrors to show what is happening above.
90676.m: You look out of a submarine through a periscope.

90677.q: What was the name of the submersible that dived to the deepest point in 1960?
90677.e: The submersible Trieste was designed by Auguste Piccard. In 1960 it reached the bottom of the Mariana Trench.
90677.m: The Trieste dived to the deepest point in 1960.

90678.q: In which Swiss lake did a tourist submarine operate from 1964?
90678.e: At the 1964 national exhibition in Lausanne, the submarine “Auguste Piccard” took visitors into Lake Geneva. It was the world's first passenger submarine.
90678.m: A tourist submarine operated in Lake Geneva in 1964.

90679.q: What do research submersibles use to collect samples from the seabed?
90679.e: Research submersibles have a robotic arm. With it they carefully pick up stones and animals.
90679.m: Submersibles collect samples with a robotic arm.

90680.q: What does a diver usually breathe from their tank?
90680.e: A diving tank usually contains completely normal air. It is tightly compressed so that a lot fits in.

90681.q: What does a diver wear on their feet?
90681.e: With flippers you move much faster underwater. They look like duck feet.
90681.m: Divers wear flippers on their feet.

90682.q: Why does a diver wear a mask over their eyes?
a: So they do not get cold
90682.e: Without a mask everything looks blurry underwater. With air in front of your eyes, you can see clearly.
90682.m: With a diving mask you can see clearly underwater.

90683.q: What is a neoprene wetsuit for?
90683.e: Water cools the body down quickly. A neoprene suit keeps the diver warm.

90684.q: What is an important rule in diving?
90684.e: Divers always go into the water with a buddy. That way they can help each other.

90685.q: Why must a diver come up slowly?
90685.e: If you come up too fast, bubbles form in the blood. That can make you ill.

90686.q: Which Frenchman became famous for films about the underwater world?
90686.e: Jacques-Yves Cousteau explored the oceans and made many films. He also helped develop modern diving equipment.
90686.m: Jacques-Yves Cousteau showed the underwater world in films.

90687.e: You cannot speak underwater. That is why divers use agreed hand signals.
90687.m: Divers talk underwater with hand signals.

90688.q: Roughly how long can a blue whale grow?
90688.e: Large blue whales grow up to about 30 metres long. That is as long as two or three buses in a row.
90688.m: A blue whale grows up to about 30 metres long.

90689.q: What does a blue whale have in its mouth instead of teeth?
90689.e: Baleen is made of long horny plates like a comb. The whale uses it to sieve its food out of the water.
90689.m: The blue whale has baleen instead of teeth.

90690.q: What does a young blue whale drink?
90690.e: The baby whale drinks its mother's rich, fatty milk. It grows very fast on it.
90690.m: A young blue whale drinks milk.

90691.q: How do blue whales communicate over long distances?
90691.e: Blue whales are among the loudest animals in the world. Their deep calls can be heard very far away in the sea.
90691.m: Blue whales call with loud, deep sounds.

90692.q: What colour is a blue whale?
90692.e: The blue whale is bluish grey with pale spots. Underwater it often looks truly blue.
90692.m: The blue whale is bluish grey.

90693.q: What does an octopus have on its arms?
90693.e: There are many suckers on its arms. The octopus uses them to hold on to prey and to feel and taste.
90693.m: Octopuses have suckers on their arms.

90694.q: What does an octopus squirt out when in danger?
90694.e: The octopus releases a dark cloud of ink. Behind it, it can quickly escape.
90694.m: Octopuses escape behind a cloud of ink.

90695.q: How does an octopus camouflage itself?
90695.e: Octopuses can change colour and pattern in a flash. That way they look like stones or sand.
90695.m: Octopuses camouflage themselves by changing colour.

90696.q: What can an octopus learn to do, for example?
a: Open a jar with a lid
90696.e: Octopuses are thought to be very clever. In experiments they have learned to open screw-top jars.

90697.q: Why can an octopus fit through very narrow gaps?
90697.e: An octopus's body is soft and has no skeleton. So it can make itself very thin.

90698.q: What does an octopus use to break up its prey?
90698.e: In the middle, between its arms, the octopus has a hard beak. With it, it can even crack crabs and mussels.

90699.q: What are jellyfish mostly made of?
90699.e: Jellyfish are about 98 per cent water. That is why they are so see-through and soft.

90700.e: The jellyfish squeezes its bell together and pushes water out. This moves it forwards.
90700.m: Jellyfish swim by squeezing their bell together.

90701.q: Which sea animal likes to eat jellyfish?
90701.e: Sea turtles like eating jellyfish. Sadly, they sometimes mistake plastic bags for jellyfish.

a: No, it has no bones and no fins
Yes, it is a small fish
Yes, it is a baby fish
90702.e: Jellyfish are neither fish nor plants. They are animals without bones, like corals and sea anemones.

90703.q: Is it OK to touch a dead jellyfish on the beach?
a: Yes, it is even as soft as cotton wool
Yes, but only with wet hands
90703.e: Even dead jellyfish can still sting. So it is better not to touch them.

90704.q: Are there jellyfish in Swiss lakes too?
a: Only in the ice in winter
90704.e: The freshwater jellyfish lives in some Swiss lakes. It grows to about 2 centimetres at most and is harmless to people.
90704.m: There are small jellyfish in Swiss lakes too.

90705.q: What can a starfish do if it loses an arm?
a: It lives without the arm for ever
It swaps it with another one
90705.e: Starfish can grow back lost arms. But it takes a long time.

90706.q: What does a starfish use to move?
90706.e: On the underside of its arms, a starfish has hundreds of tiny feet. With them it crawls slowly forwards.
90706.m: Starfish crawl on lots of tube feet.

90707.q: What does a starfish like to eat?
90707.e: The starfish pulls mussels open with its little feet. Then it eats the soft animal inside.

90708.q: Where does a starfish have simple eyes?
a: At the tips of its arms
90708.e: There is a small eye at the tip of each arm. With it, the starfish can tell light from dark.
90708.m: Starfish have eyes at the tips of their arms.

90709.q: What flows through many tubes in a starfish instead of blood?
90709.e: A starfish does not have blood like ours. Sea water flows through its body in fine tubes.
90709.m: Sea water flows through a starfish.

90710.q: What happens at the seaside at low tide?
90710.e: At low tide the sea level falls. The water draws back from the beach.
90710.m: At low tide the sea goes out.

90711.q: What happens at the seaside at high tide?
90711.e: At high tide the sea level rises. The water comes far up the beach.
90711.m: At high tide the water rises.

90712.e: The Moon pulls on the Earth's water with its gravity. This creates the tides.

90713.q: Roughly how often is there a high tide in one day?
90713.e: On most coasts there are two high tides and two low tides a day. They take turns.
90713.m: There are about two high tides a day.

90714.q: What is the seabed on the North Sea coast that lies dry at low tide called?
90714.e: At low tide you can walk around on the mudflats. Worms, mussels and crabs live there.
90714.m: At low tide the mudflats on the North Sea lie dry.

90715.q: Can you notice the tides on Lake Geneva?
90715.e: Tides are only clearly noticeable in the great oceans. In lakes like Lake Geneva, you hardly notice them.
90715.m: There are hardly any tides in Swiss lakes.

90716.q: When are the tides especially strong?
a: At full moon and new moon
90716.e: At full moon and new moon, the Sun and Moon pull in a line. Then the difference is greatest.
90716.m: The tides are strong at full moon and new moon.

90717.q: Roughly how long does it take from high tide to low tide?
90717.e: It takes just over 6 hours from high water to low water. Then the water rises again.
90717.m: It takes about 6 hours from high tide to low tide.

90718.q: What does sea water taste like?
90718.e: A lot of salt is dissolved in sea water. That is why it tastes salty.

90719.q: Can you drink sea water when you are thirsty?
a: No, it makes you even thirstier
Yes, but only in the morning
90719.e: The body needs a lot of water to get rid of the salt again. That is why sea water makes you even thirstier.
90719.m: Sea water does not quench your thirst.

90720.q: Where does most of the salt in the sea come from?
90720.e: Rain and rivers dissolve tiny amounts of salt from rocks. Over a very long time, the rivers carry it into the sea.
90720.m: The salt in the sea comes from rocks.

90721.q: Which sea in Europe is only slightly salty?
90721.e: Many rivers with fresh water flow into the Baltic Sea. That is why its water is much less salty than ocean water.
90721.m: The Baltic Sea is only slightly salty.

90722.q: In which salty body of water can you float on top without any effort?
90722.e: The Dead Sea is about ten times saltier than normal sea water. That is why you do not sink there.
90722.m: You do not sink in the Dead Sea.

90723.q: Where does the salt that is taken from the ground in Switzerland come from?
90723.e: A very long time ago, a sea covered parts of Switzerland. When it evaporated, salt was left behind in the ground.
90723.m: Swiss salt comes from an ancient sea.

90724.q: At what temperature does sea water freeze?
90724.e: Salt in water lowers the freezing point. Sea water only freezes at about minus 2 degrees.
90724.m: Sea water only freezes below 0 degrees.

90725.q: What does the anglerfish use its glow for?
90725.e: The anglerfish has a glowing lure on its head, like a fishing rod. Small fish swim towards the light and get eaten.
90725.m: The anglerfish lures prey with light.

90726.q: What is it called when living things make their own light?
90726.e: Many deep sea animals make their own light. This is called bioluminescence.
90726.m: Light made by living things is called bioluminescence.

90727.q: What is it called when the sea glows bluish in the waves at night?
90727.e: Tiny living things in the water light up when the water moves. This is called sea sparkle.
90727.m: In sea sparkle, tiny living things in the water glow.

90728.q: What makes the light in the glowing lure of many anglerfish?
90728.e: Tiny bacteria that glow live in the lure. In return, the fish gives them a place to live.
90728.m: Glowing bacteria make the anglerfish's light.

90729.q: What colour is the light of many deep sea animals usually?
90729.e: Blue light travels furthest in water. That is why many deep sea animals glow blue.
90729.m: Many deep sea animals glow blue.

90730.q: Which deep sea fish is named after a lamp?
90730.e: Lanternfish have lots of small glowing spots on their bodies. They are among the most common fish in the deep sea.
90730.m: The lanternfish has glowing spots on its body.

90731.q: Why do many deep sea fish have a huge mouth?
a: They need a lot of air
90731.e: There is little to eat in the deep sea. With a big mouth they can grab any prey, even large prey.
90731.m: Deep sea fish often have a big mouth.

90732.q: Which animal on land also makes its own light?
90732.e: Like deep sea fish, glow-worms make their own light. You can see them glowing on summer nights.
90732.m: Glow-worms make their own light too.

90733.q: According to Swiss advice, how often at most should you eat meat?
90733.e: The Swiss dietary guidelines advise eating meat and sausage at most 2 to 3 times a week. On the other days you can have eggs, fish or tofu, for example.
90733.m: Meat is eaten only a few times a week.

90734.q: What is at the very top of the food pyramid?
90734.e: The top is very narrow. Sweet things and salty snacks should only be eaten rarely and in small amounts.
90734.m: The top of the pyramid shows what you should eat only rarely.

90735.q: Why is the food pyramid so wide at the bottom?
a: You should eat most of that
You should eat least of that
That is where the most expensive food is
90735.e: The wider a level is, the more of it you should eat or drink. At the top the pyramid gets narrow; that is where the things you need only a little of are.
90735.m: Wide levels mean a lot, narrow levels mean a little.

90736.q: How many portions of cereals or potatoes does the Swiss pyramid recommend per day?
90736.e: The Swiss dietary guidelines advise 3 portions a day from this group, for example bread, pasta, rice or potatoes.
90736.m: Three portions of cereals or potatoes a day give you energy.

90737.q: How many portions of dairy products does the Swiss food pyramid recommend per day?
90737.e: 2 to 3 portions of milk or dairy products a day are recommended. One portion is, for example, a glass of milk or a yoghurt.
90737.m: Two to three portions of dairy products a day are enough.

90738.q: Which group is directly above drinks in the food pyramid?
90738.e: Just above the drinks comes the second wide level with vegetables and fruit. So you should eat a lot of them.
90738.m: Vegetables and fruit are near the bottom of the pyramid.

90739.q: Which vegetable oil do the Swiss dietary guidelines especially recommend?
90739.e: The guidelines advise at least one tablespoon of rapeseed oil a day. Rapeseed is also grown in Switzerland.
90739.m: Rapeseed oil is a healthy cooking oil.

90740.q: How many tablespoons of vegetable oil does the Swiss pyramid recommend per day?
90740.e: About 2 tablespoons of vegetable oil a day are recommended, for example rapeseed oil for salad. The body needs oil in small amounts.
90740.m: A little vegetable oil every day is healthy.

90741.q: How many portions of meat, fish, eggs or tofu does the Swiss pyramid recommend per day?
90741.e: 1 portion of a protein-rich food a day is recommended. You should vary it.
90741.m: One portion of protein a day is enough.

90742.q: Which of these foods is a vegetable?
90742.e: The cucumber is a vegetable. Apples, pears and grapes are fruit.

90743.q: Which vegetable is orange and grows in the ground?
90743.e: The carrot is the orange root of the plant and grows underground. In Switzerland it is also called Rüebli.
90743.m: The carrot grows in the ground as an orange root.

90744.q: Which vegetable often makes your eyes water when you cut it?
90744.e: When you cut an onion, a substance is released that stings the eyes. That is why your eyes water.

90745.q: Which green vegetable looks like little trees?
90745.e: Broccoli has lots of small green florets on thick stalks. That is why it looks like little trees.
90745.m: Broccoli looks like a little forest.

90746.q: What colour is a ripe tomato usually?
90746.e: Ripe tomatoes are usually red. But there are also yellow and green varieties.

90747.q: What is lamb's lettuce, called Nüsslisalat in Switzerland?
a: A salad with small green leaves
90747.e: Lamb's lettuce has small dark green leaves and also grows in winter. Its Swiss name contains the word for nut, but it has nothing to do with nuts; it just tastes a little nutty.
90747.m: Lamb's lettuce is a salad with small leaves.

90748.q: Which vegetable is dark red and stains your hands when you cut it?
90748.e: Beetroot has a strong red colouring. It stains your hands and the chopping board red.

90749.q: Which vegetable is sauerkraut made from?
90749.e: Sauerkraut is made from finely shredded white cabbage that turns sour with salt. In Switzerland white cabbage is also called Kabis.
90749.m: Sauerkraut is made from white cabbage.

90750.q: Which fruit is yellow and curved?
90750.e: The banana has a yellow skin and is curved. It grows in warm countries.
90750.m: The banana is yellow and curved.

90751.q: Because of its many fruit trees, Thurgau is jokingly called “Mostindien” (“Cider India”). Which fruit grows there especially often?
90751.e: There are very many apple trees in Thurgau. A lot of apple juice and cider is made from the apples there.
90751.m: Thurgau is known for its apples.

90752.q: Which fruit is a citrus fruit?
90752.e: Like the lemon and the mandarin, the orange is a citrus fruit. It has a lot of vitamin C.
90752.m: The orange is a citrus fruit.

90753.q: Which small red fruit has a hard stone in the middle?
90753.e: The cherry is a stone fruit. In the middle there is a hard stone that you don't eat.
90753.m: The cherry has a hard stone.

90754.q: Which fruit is brown and hairy outside and green inside?
90754.e: The kiwi has a brown, hairy skin. Inside it is green with lots of tiny black seeds.
90754.m: The kiwi is brown outside and green inside.

90755.q: Which small blue berry grows on low bushes in the woods?
90755.e: Bilberries grow on low bushes, including in Swiss woods. They are also called wild blueberries.

90756.q: Why should you wash fruit before eating it?
90756.e: There can be soil, dust and sprays on the skin. You wash them off with water.
90756.m: Wash fruit before you eat it.

90757.q: When are there fresh strawberries from the fields in Switzerland?
90757.e: Swiss strawberries are mainly picked in May, June and July. None grow outdoors in winter.
90757.m: Strawberries from the fields come in early summer.

90758.q: What is wholemeal bread made from?
90758.e: For wholemeal flour, the whole grain is ground, including the outer layer and the germ. Wholemeal bread is baked from it.
90758.m: Wholemeal bread contains the whole grain.

90759.q: What does wholemeal bread have more of than white bread?
90759.e: Wholemeal bread contains a lot of fibre. It is good for digestion.
90759.m: Wholemeal bread has a lot of fibre.

90760.q: Which ancient grain is related to wheat and popular in Switzerland for making bread?
90760.e: Spelt is an ancient kind of wheat. It has been grown in Switzerland for a long time and baked into bread.
90760.m: Spelt is an ancient bread grain.

90761.q: What colour is wholemeal bread usually?
90761.e: Because the dark outer layer of the grain is ground in too, wholemeal bread is usually brown.

90762.q: Which grain is most bread in Switzerland baked from?
90762.e: In Switzerland wheat is the most important bread grain. Wheat flour is used, for example, to bake Zopf plaited bread and Weggli rolls.
90762.m: Wheat is Switzerland's most important bread grain.

90763.q: Which parts of the grain are missing from white flour?
a: The outer layer and the germ
90763.e: For white flour, only the light-coloured inside of the grain is ground. The outer layer and the germ are removed.
90763.m: White flour has no outer layer and no germ.

90764.q: Which group of the food pyramid does wholemeal bread belong to?
90764.e: Bread is made from cereal grains. It belongs to the group with cereal products and potatoes.

90765.q: According to the guidelines, how many of the daily cereal portions should be wholegrain?
90765.e: The Swiss dietary guidelines advise eating at least half of your cereal products as wholegrain.
90765.m: At least half of your cereals should be wholegrain.

90766.q: Which of these foods is a dairy product?
90766.e: Quark is made from milk. Rice, honey and bread don't have milk as their main ingredient.

90767.q: What is the yellowish liquid left over when cheese is made called?
90767.e: When cheese is made, the milk separates into solid curds and liquid whey. The whey is often fed to pigs or made into drinks.
90767.m: Whey is left over when cheese is made.

90768.q: Which animal does most milk in Switzerland come from?
90768.e: Almost all the milk in Switzerland comes from cows. But there is also goat's and sheep's milk.
90768.m: Most milk in Switzerland comes from cows.

90769.q: Which well-known Swiss cheese has big holes?
90769.e: Emmentaler is famous for its big round holes. It comes from the Emmental valley in the canton of Bern.

90770.q: What do you get if you whip cream for a very long time?
90770.e: First the cream becomes whipped cream. If you keep going, the fat separates and you get butter.
90770.m: Cream whipped for a long time turns into butter.

90772.q: Which Swiss cheese dish is eaten from a shared pot?
90772.e: For fondue, cheese is melted in a special pot called a caquelon. Everyone dips their bread on a fork into the shared pot.
90772.m: Fondue is eaten together from one pot.

90773.q: Where do you keep an opened carton of milk?
90773.e: Milk stays fresh for longer in the fridge. In the warmth it soon goes sour.
90773.m: Opened milk belongs in the fridge.

90774.q: What should you do after eating sweets?
90774.e: After brushing your teeth, fewer bits of sugar stay on them. That keeps your teeth healthy.
90774.m: After sweet things it is best to brush your teeth.

90775.q: Which plant is sugar made from in Switzerland?
90775.e: In Switzerland sugar is made from sugar beet, for example in the factories in Aarberg and Frauenfeld.
90775.m: Swiss sugar comes from sugar beet.

90776.q: How many sweet things per day does the Swiss food pyramid recommend at most?
90776.e: Sweet things are in the narrow top. You can enjoy them, but at most one small portion a day.
90776.m: Sweet things are allowed, but only a little.

90777.q: Which sweet food do bees make?
90777.e: Bees collect nectar from flowers and turn it into honey. Honey contains a lot of sugar.

90778.q: What are the white, airy bakes made of egg white and sugar, which people in Switzerland like to eat with cream?
90778.e: Meringues are baked from whipped egg white and sugar. They are especially well known in the Bernese Oberland.
90778.m: Meringues are made of egg white and sugar.

90779.q: Which biscuit is a famous sweet treat from Basel?
90779.e: Basler Läckerli are small, hard gingerbread biscuits with honey and spices. They are a speciality of Basel.

90781.q: Which meal do you eat before the Znüni?
90781.e: First, in the morning, comes breakfast, called Zmorge in Swiss German. Later in the morning comes the Znüni.
90781.m: The Zmorge comes before the Znüni.

90783.q: Which fruit is especially easy to peel by hand for a mid-morning snack?
90783.e: You can peel a mandarin without a knife and split it into segments. That is why it is good for break time.
90783.m: A mandarin is a handy mid-morning snack.

90784.q: Why are crisps not a good mid-morning snack?
a: They have lots of fat and salt
90784.e: Crisps contain a lot of fat and salt but few vitamins. They don't keep you full for long.
90784.m: Crisps are not a good mid-morning snack.

90785.q: When do you usually eat your Znüni at school?
90785.e: Many schools have a long break in the morning. That is when the children eat their Znüni.
90785.m: The Znüni is eaten at morning break.

90786.q: Why is a mid-morning snack a good idea?
a: It gives energy for the morning
90786.e: It is a long time until lunch. A small snack helps you concentrate well.
90786.m: A mid-morning snack gives new energy for the morning.

90787.q: What is the best thing to bring your mid-morning snack to school in?
90787.e: In a snack box the food stays clean and does not get squashed. You can use the box again and again.
90787.m: A snack box protects your snack.

90788.q: Which vegetable is good to nibble raw as a mid-morning snack?
90788.e: Carrots can be eaten raw and are good to nibble. Raw potatoes are not eaten.
90788.m: Carrots make a tasty snack to nibble.

90789.q: What is a classic Swiss Zvieri?
a: Bread and a piece of chocolate
90789.e: A piece of bread with a little chocolate is a typical Zvieri in Switzerland. Rösti, fondue and raclette are main meals.
90789.m: Bread and chocolate are a typical Zvieri.

90791.q: What makes a good healthy afternoon snack?
90791.e: Yoghurt with fruit gives energy and vitamins. Jelly sweets and lemonade have a lot of sugar.
90791.m: Yoghurt with fruit is a good afternoon snack.

90792.q: Why should the afternoon snack be fairly small?
a: So you are still hungry in the evening
90792.e: A small afternoon snack takes away the hunger in the afternoon. Then you still have an appetite for dinner.
90792.m: A small afternoon snack leaves room for dinner.

90793.q: Which meal comes after the Zvieri?
90793.e: After the Zvieri in the afternoon comes dinner in the evening, called Znacht in Swiss German.

90794.q: Which afternoon snack provides a lot of protein?
90794.e: Cheese is made from milk and contains a lot of protein. Squash, sweets and cucumbers have hardly any protein.

90795.q: Which afternoon snack is healthy and crunchy?
a: Vegetable sticks with a quark dip
90795.e: Vegetable sticks such as cucumber or pepper give you vitamins. With a quark dip they taste even better.
90795.m: Vegetable sticks make a crunchy afternoon snack.

90796.q: Lunch is at 12 o'clock and the Zvieri at 4 pm (16:00). How many hours are there in between?
90796.e: From 12:00 to 16:00 is 16 minus 12, which is 4 hours.
90796.m: There are a few hours between lunch and the Zvieri.

90797.q: Where does most drinking water in Switzerland come from?
90797.e: About four fifths of Swiss drinking water comes from springs and groundwater. The rest comes mainly from lakes.
90797.m: Most Swiss drinking water comes from the ground.

90798.q: How can you always have water with you when you are out?
90798.e: You can fill a water bottle with tap water at home and take it with you. That way you can always have a drink.
90798.m: Always take a water bottle with you.

90799.q: How much unsweetened drink does the Swiss pyramid recommend for adults per day?
90799.e: 1 to 2 litres of unsweetened drinks a day are recommended, ideally water. Children need a little less.
90799.m: Adults should drink 1 to 2 litres a day.

90800.q: What is water from a protected spring that is sold in bottles called?
90800.e: Mineral water comes from protected underground springs and contains minerals. It is filled into bottles.

90801.q: What is a sign that the body needs water?
90801.e: Thirst is a signal from the body. It shows that you should drink.
90801.m: Thirst shows that you should drink.

90802.q: Which is much cheaper in Switzerland: tap water or bottled water?
90802.e: A litre of tap water in Switzerland costs only a fraction of a centime. Bottled water is much more expensive.

90803.q: From which lake does the city of Zurich get a large part of its drinking water?
90803.e: Zurich's water supply takes most of its water from Lake Zurich and treats it.
90803.m: Zurich drinks water from Lake Zurich.

90804.q: Who brings drinking water to people's homes?
90804.e: The water supply, usually run by the municipality, collects the water, checks it and sends it through pipes to the houses.
90804.m: The water supply delivers our drinking water.

90805.q: Can you drink from public fountains in Swiss towns?
a: Yes, if there is no warning sign
90805.e: Most town fountains have drinking water. Where the water is not safe to drink, there is a sign saying “Not drinking water”.
90805.m: You can drink from fountains without a warning sign.

90806.q: Roughly how much sugar is in half a litre of cola?
90806.e: Half a litre of normal cola contains over 50 grams of sugar. That is more than 10 sugar cubes.
90806.m: Sweet drinks hide a lot of sugar.

90807.q: Which drink is a sweet drink?
90807.e: Lemonade contains a lot of added sugar. Water and unsweetened tea have no sugar.

90808.q: What is the tooth disease called that can be caused by lots of sugar?
90808.e: Tooth decay makes holes in the teeth. People who often have sweet drinks are more likely to get tooth decay.
90808.m: Too much sugar can cause tooth decay.

90809.q: What is a good alternative to sweet drinks?
a: Water with a slice of lemon
90809.e: A slice of lemon gives water flavour without much sugar. That keeps the drink healthy.
90809.m: Water with lemon is a tasty thirst-quencher.

90810.e: Squash is very sweet. Well diluted with water, a glass contains less sugar.

90811.e: Herbal tea without sugar or honey contains no sugar. Iced tea, lemonade and cola are sweetened.
90811.m: Unsweetened tea is a good thirst-quencher.

90812.q: Why are energy drinks not suitable for children?
a: They have lots of caffeine and sugar
90812.e: Energy drinks contain a lot of caffeine and sugar. This is not healthy for children; it can cause a racing heart and sleep problems, for example.
90812.m: Energy drinks are not for children.

90813.q: What makes the bubbles in many sweet drinks?
90813.e: Many sweet drinks contain carbon dioxide. It makes the fizzy bubbles.
90813.m: Carbon dioxide makes the bubbles in drinks.

90814.q: Do frozen vegetables count towards your “5 a day”?
90814.e: Frozen vegetables count too. They are frozen soon after harvest and keep many good nutrients.

90815.q: How many of the five daily portions should be vegetables?
90815.e: 3 portions of vegetables plus fruit are recommended. So vegetables should make up the bigger part.
90815.m: More vegetables than fruit is ideal.

90816.q: Roughly how big is one portion for “5 a day”?
90816.e: One portion is about a handful. Children have smaller hands, so their portions are smaller.
90816.m: One portion roughly fits in your own hand.

90817.q: Which is healthier: a whole apple or a glass of apple juice?
90817.e: The 2024 Swiss dietary guidelines focus on whole fruit. It has more fibre and keeps you full longer than juice.
90817.m: Whole fruit is better than juice.

90818.q: Why should you eat vegetables and fruit in lots of colours?
a: Each colour has different good substances
90818.e: Different colours show different plant substances and vitamins. If you eat lots of colours, you get lots of them.

90819.q: What is the best way to manage your “5 a day”?
a: Some vegetables or fruit with every meal
All at once in the evening
90819.e: If you eat some vegetables or fruit with every meal and with your mid-morning and afternoon snacks, five portions soon add up.
90819.m: Every meal should include some vegetables or fruit.

90820.q: Which mid-morning snack helps with your “5 a day”?
90820.e: Apple slices are a portion of fruit. Crisps, biscuits and jelly sweets don't count.
90820.m: Fruit as a mid-morning snack helps with your “5 a day”.

90821.q: Do potatoes count towards the five portions of vegetables and fruit?
90821.e: In the pyramid, potatoes belong to the group with bread, rice and pasta. That is why they don't count towards “5 a day”.
90821.m: Potatoes don't count towards “5 a day”.

90822.e: Lentils grow in small pods. That is why they are pulses.

90823.q: What do peas grow in on the plant?
90823.e: Peas grow in green pods. Inside, the peas lie in a row.

90824.q: Which pulse is the main ingredient of hummus?
90824.e: Hummus is a paste made from cooked chickpeas. It comes from the Middle East.

90825.q: What do pulses contain especially a lot of?
90825.e: Pulses have a lot of protein and fibre. That is why they can replace meat.
90825.m: Pulses provide a lot of protein.

90826.e: Lentils are pulses. They make lentil soup hearty and keep you full for a long time.

90827.q: Do dried beans have to be cooked before you eat them?
90827.e: Raw beans contain substances that can give you tummy ache. Cooking destroys them.

90828.q: Which pulse is tofu made from?
90828.e: Tofu is made from soya milk, and soya milk from soya beans. Tofu originally comes from China.
90828.m: Tofu is made from soya beans.

90829.q: Which pulse goes into chilli con carne?
90829.e: Chilli con carne has red kidney beans in it. It also has minced meat, tomatoes and chilli.

90830.q: Which pulse is small, round and green?
90830.e: Peas are small, round, green balls. They are often eaten together with carrots.
90830.m: Peas are small, round and green.

90831.q: In German music notation, which note name comes after A?
90831.e: In German, the notes are called C, D, E, F, G, A and then H. In English this note is called B.
90831.m: In German, H comes after A.

90832.q: How many different natural notes are there from C to B?
90832.e: The natural notes are C, D, E, F, G, A and B. That is seven notes, and then it starts again with C.

90833.q: What is a row of notes that gets higher step by step called?
90833.e: A scale goes up or down step by step, like a ladder.
90833.m: A scale goes step by step.

90834.q: What is the difference between a musical note and a noise?
a: A note has a clear pitch
90834.e: You can sing a note because it has a definite pitch. A noise such as rustling has no clear pitch.
90834.m: A note has a definite pitch, a noise does not.

90835.q: What is the sign called that you use to write down a note?
90835.e: Music is written down with notes. The position of the note on the stave shows which note is meant.
90835.m: You write down sounds with notes.

90836.q: What is the distance from one C to the next higher C called?
90836.e: The octave is the distance between two notes with the same name. The higher one sounds very similar, just brighter.
90836.m: Two notes with the same name are an octave apart.

90837.q: Which syllables can you use to sing a scale?
90837.e: With the syllables Do, Re, Mi, Fa, So, La, Ti you can sing the notes of a scale.
90837.m: Do, Re, Mi are singing syllables for the scale.

90838.q: What do you call someone who invents and writes down pieces of music?
90838.e: A composer invents music and writes it down in notes. The conductor leads an orchestra.

90839.q: Who usually has the higher voice?
90839.e: Children have small vocal cords. That is why their voices sound higher than a grown man's.

90840.q: Which animal squeaks with a high voice?
90840.e: The mouse is small and squeaks high. Big animals such as cows or bears tend to make deep grumbling sounds.

90841.q: What happens when you sing up a scale?
90841.e: When singing up, each note is a little higher than the one before.
90841.m: When singing up, the notes get higher.

90842.q: Which instrument plays the lowest notes?
90842.e: The double bass is the largest string instrument in the orchestra. It plays very low, rumbling notes.
90842.m: The double bass sounds very low.

90843.q: What is the highest female voice in a choir called?
90843.e: In a choir, women and children sing soprano or alto. Soprano is the highest voice.
90843.m: Soprano is the highest voice in the choir.

90844.q: Which is higher: the cheep of a bird or the rumble of a lorry?
90844.e: Birds chirp with bright, high notes. A lorry engine rumbles low.
90844.m: Bird calls are high, engines rumble low.

90845.q: A siren wails low, then high. What is changing?
90845.e: The siren switches between low and high notes. So it is the pitch that changes.
90845.m: With a siren, the pitch changes.

90846.q: Where does a high note sit on the stave?
90846.e: The higher a note sounds, the higher up its note sits on the lines.
90846.m: High notes sit high on the stave.

90847.q: What do you play a guitar with?
90847.e: The guitar strings are plucked or strummed with the fingers or a small pick.
90847.m: You play the guitar by plucking the strings.

90848.q: What is the small flat piece you strike guitar strings with called?
90848.e: The plectrum is a small flat piece of plastic. You hold it between your thumb and index finger.
90848.m: You strike the strings with the plectrum.

90849.q: What is the round hole in the wooden body of a guitar called?
90849.e: The sound comes out of the hollow body of the guitar through the sound hole.
90849.m: The guitar has a sound hole.

90850.q: What does the hollow wooden body of the guitar do to the sound?
90850.e: The hollow body vibrates too and amplifies the sound of the strings. Without it the guitar would be very quiet.
90850.m: The guitar body amplifies the sound.

90851.q: What are the metal strips across the neck of the guitar called?
90851.e: The frets divide the neck into sections. If you press a string behind a fret, you get a particular note.
90851.m: The frets show where to press.

90852.q: Why do you turn the pegs at the top of the guitar neck?
90852.e: With the pegs you tighten or loosen the strings. That is how you tune the guitar.
90852.m: You tune the guitar with the pegs.

90853.q: What are the hairs of a violin bow usually made of?
90853.e: The bow hairs are usually tail hairs from horses. They are also called horsehair.
90853.m: Violin bows have hairs from horses.

90854.q: What do you rub on the bow hairs so they grip the strings better?
90854.e: Rosin is a solid resin. It makes the bow hairs grippy so that the string vibrates.

90855.q: Which large string instrument do you put between your knees to play?
90855.e: The cello is much bigger than the violin. You play it sitting down, and it stands on the floor on a spike.
90855.m: You play the cello sitting down.

90856.q: What is another name for the fiddle?
90856.e: Violin is the proper name for the fiddle. In the orchestra, many violins play together.
90856.m: The fiddle is also called a violin.

90857.q: Which group of instruments does the violin belong to?
90857.e: On the violin, you draw the bow across the strings. That is why it belongs to the string instruments.
90857.m: The violin is a string instrument.

90858.q: Which flute do many children in Switzerland learn at school?
90858.e: The recorder is small, cheap and easy to learn. That is why many children play it at school.

90859.q: What vibrates in a flute and makes the sound?
90859.e: In a flute, your breath makes the air in the tube vibrate. That is how the sound is made.
90859.m: In a flute, the air vibrates.

90860.q: What happens to the note when you cover more holes on a recorder?
90860.e: With more holes closed, a longer column of air vibrates. That is why the note sounds lower.
90860.m: More fingers on the holes give lower notes.

90861.q: Which group of instruments does the flute belong to?
90861.e: On a flute, the sound is made by blowing into it. That is why it is a wind instrument.
90861.m: The flute is a wind instrument.

90862.q: What can a recorder be made of?
90862.e: Recorders are made from different kinds of wood or from plastic. Plastic recorders are cheap and easy to clean.
90862.m: Recorders are made of wood or plastic.

90863.q: Which recorder is smaller and sounds higher?
90863.e: The soprano recorder is the usual school recorder. It is smaller than the alto recorder and sounds higher.
90863.m: The soprano recorder sounds higher than the alto recorder.

90864.q: The transverse flute is usually made of metal. Which group does it still belong to?
90864.e: Flutes used to be made of wood. Also, their sound is made in the same way as on a wooden flute, so they count as woodwind instruments.
90864.m: The flute is a woodwind instrument.

90865.q: Which small, very high flute do many people play at the Basel Carnival?
90865.e: At the Basel Carnival, groups called cliques march through the streets with drums and piccolos. The piccolo is a small transverse flute.
90865.m: At the Basel Carnival, people play the piccolo.

90866.q: What are the bars of a xylophone made of?
90866.e: The word comes from the Greek “xylon”, which means wood. The bars are made of hard wood.

90867.q: What do you play a xylophone with?
90867.e: You strike the wooden bars with small mallets. The mallets have a ball at the end.
90867.m: You play the xylophone with mallets.

90868.q: Which bar of a xylophone sounds the highest?
90868.e: Short bars vibrate faster than long ones. That is why the shortest bar sounds the highest.

90869.q: Which group of instruments does the xylophone belong to?
90869.e: On a xylophone, the sound is made by striking. That is why it counts as a percussion instrument.
90869.m: The xylophone is a percussion instrument.

90870.q: What is a similar instrument with metal bars called?
90870.e: On a metallophone, the bars are made of metal instead of wood. It sounds brighter and rings longer.

90871.q: What are the tubes under the bars of a large xylophone for?
90871.e: The tubes vibrate along and amplify the sound. They are called resonator tubes.
90871.m: Tubes under the bars amplify the sound.

90872.q: What is a large xylophone with a deep, soft sound called?
90872.e: The marimba is a large wooden instrument with bars. It sounds deeper and softer than a small xylophone.
90872.m: The marimba is a large xylophone.

90873.q: With which mallets does a xylophone sound softer?
90873.e: A soft head made of rubber or wool softens the stroke. Hard mallets sound bright and sharp.
90873.m: Soft mallets give a soft sound.

90874.q: What is the part inside a bell that strikes the side called?
90874.e: The clapper hangs inside the bell. When the bell swings, it strikes the rim and the bell rings.
90874.m: The clapper makes the bell ring.

90875.q: In Switzerland, what is a large cowbell made of hammered sheet metal called?
90875.e: A Treichel is hammered out of sheet metal. It sounds deep and booming.
90875.m: A Treichel is a large cowbell made of sheet metal.

90876.q: Why do cows on Alpine pastures wear bells?
a: So that people can hear and find them
So that they don't get cold
90876.e: On large pastures and in fog, you cannot always see the cows. The farmer can hear where they are from the sound of the bells.
90876.m: Cowbells help people find the cows.

90877.e: Big, heavy bells vibrate more slowly. That is why they sound lower than small bells.

90878.q: In which custom in the Engadine do children walk through the village with bells to drive away winter?
90878.e: At Chalandamarz on 1 March, children in the Engadine walk through the villages with bells. The noise is meant to drive away winter.
90878.m: At Chalandamarz, children ring winter away.

90879.q: What happens to the sound of a bell if you hold it with your hand?
90879.e: Your hand stops the bell from vibrating. That is why the sound quickly dies away.
90879.m: A bell that is held goes quiet.

90880.q: What is the bell at the front door called?
90880.e: Visitors use the doorbell to let you know they are there. Today it is usually electric.
90880.m: At the front door there is a doorbell.

90881.q: What are bells usually made of?
90881.e: Metal keeps vibrating for a long time after it is struck. That is why metal bells sound bright and ring for a long time.
90881.m: Bells are usually made of metal.

90882.q: Which metal are church bells usually made of?
90882.e: Church bells are usually made of bronze. This metal sounds very beautiful and rings for a long time.
90882.m: Church bells are usually made of bronze.

90883.q: How is a church bell made?
90883.e: The liquid metal is poured into a mould. After it cools, the bell is dug out and cleaned.

90884.q: How heavy can a large church bell be?
90884.e: Large church bells are made of thick metal. Some weigh as much as several cars put together.
90884.m: Large church bells are very heavy.

90885.q: Where does the Zurich Sechseläuten get its name from?
a: From bells ringing at six o'clock
90885.e: In the past, a bell rang at six in the evening in summer to mark the end of the working day. That is where the name Sechseläuten (“six o'clock ringing”) comes from.
90885.m: The Sechseläuten is named after the ringing of a bell.

90886.q: What do many church bells show every hour, on the hour?
90886.e: Many church clocks strike the hours with a bell. At three o'clock it strikes three times.
90886.m: The church bell strikes the hours.

90887.q: When do church bells often ring for a long time on Sundays?
90887.e: The ringing before the service calls people to church.
90887.m: The bells ring before the church service.

90888.q: What strikes the strings inside a piano?
90888.e: When you press a key, a small felt hammer strikes the strings. Then the note sounds.
90888.m: In a piano, hammers strike the strings.

90889.q: On which side of the piano are the high notes?
90889.e: From left to right, the notes on the piano get higher and higher.
90889.m: On the piano, the high notes are on the right.

90890.q: What is a large piano with horizontal strings and a lid that opens called?
90890.e: In a grand piano, the strings lie horizontally. It is bigger than an ordinary piano and often stands on concert stages.
90890.m: A grand piano is a large piano.

90891.q: What does a piano have pedals for?
90891.e: With the right pedal, the notes ring on for longer. With the left pedal, the piano sounds quieter.
90891.m: You change the sound with the pedals.

90892.q: What do you call someone who plays the piano?
90892.e: Pianist comes from piano, the Italian word for this instrument.

90893.q: How are the black keys on a piano arranged?
a: In groups of two and three
90893.e: The black keys alternate between groups of two and three keys. This helps you find your way around the piano.
90893.m: Black keys form groups of two and three.

90894.q: What kind of instrument is the Schwyzerörgeli?
90894.e: The Schwyzerörgeli is a small button accordion. It is typical of Swiss folk music.
90894.m: The Schwyzerörgeli is a small accordion.

90895.q: What do you pull and push on an Örgeli so that air flows through it?
90895.e: The bellows in the middle are folded like a concertina. When you pull and push, air flows through the instrument.
90895.m: The bellows blow air through the Örgeli.

90896.q: In which kind of music is the Schwyzerörgeli often played?
90896.e: The Schwyzerörgeli belongs to Swiss folk music, especially Ländler music.
90896.m: The Schwyzerörgeli is played in Ländler music.

90897.q: How do you hold a Schwyzerörgeli when playing?
a: In front of your tummy between both hands
Under your chin like a violin
At your mouth like a flute
On your knees like a drum
90897.e: The Örgeli rests in front of your tummy. The right hand presses the melody buttons, the left hand pulls and pushes the bellows.
90897.m: You hold a Schwyzerörgeli in front of your tummy.

90898.q: How do you play a Schwyzerörgeli?
a: You press buttons and pull the bellows
90898.e: On a Schwyzerörgeli you press small buttons. At the same time you pull and push the bellows so that air flows through the instrument.
90898.m: On an Örgeli you press buttons and move the bellows.

90899.q: What is special about the melody buttons on a Schwyzerörgeli?
a: Pulling and pushing give different notes
They light up when you play
90899.e: The melody buttons are bisonoric. The same button gives a different note when pulling than when pushing.
90899.m: An Örgeli button has two notes.

90900.q: Which hand plays the bass on a Schwyzerörgeli?
90900.e: The melody buttons are on the right, the bass buttons for the accompaniment on the left. The left hand also pulls and pushes the bellows.
90900.m: The left hand plays the bass.

90901.q: What vibrates inside a Schwyzerörgeli when air flows through it?
90901.e: Inside the Örgeli there are many small metal reeds. The air makes them vibrate, and that is how the notes are made.
90901.m: In an Örgeli, metal reeds vibrate.

90902.q: How is a pan flute built?
90902.e: On a pan flute, many tubes are joined side by side. Each tube gives its own note.
90902.m: A pan flute has many tubes side by side.

90903.q: Who is the pan flute named after?
90903.e: In old Greek legends, the shepherd god Pan played on a flute like this.
90903.m: The pan flute is named after the god Pan.

90904.q: Which tube of a pan flute sounds the lowest?
90904.e: In a long tube, a lot of air vibrates. That is why the longest tube sounds the lowest.

90905.q: How do you play a pan flute?
a: You stroke it with a bow
90905.e: You blow across the top edge of a tube, a bit like blowing across an empty bottle. That makes a note.
90905.m: You play a pan flute by blowing across the edge.

90906.q: What were pan flutes usually made of in the past?
90906.e: Reed and bamboo are hollow inside. That is why they are good for the tubes of a pan flute.
90906.m: Pan flutes are made from hollow plant stems.

90907.q: In which mountain range in South America is the pan flute often played?
90907.e: In the music of the Andes, for example in Peru and Bolivia, the pan flute is very popular.
90907.m: In the Andes, people often play the pan flute.

90908.q: What are the tubes of a pan flute like at the bottom?
90908.e: The tubes are closed at the bottom. The air vibrates back and forth inside and cannot escape at the bottom.
90908.m: The tubes of a pan flute are closed at the bottom.

90909.q: How many notes does a single tube of a pan flute normally give?
90909.e: Each tube has a fixed length and so gives one note. To play a tune, you move from tube to tube.
90909.m: Each tube of a pan flute gives one note.

90910.e: A thick string is heavier and vibrates more slowly. That is why it sounds lower than a thin one.

90911.q: What happens to the note when you tighten a string more?
90911.e: A tightly stretched string vibrates faster. That is why the note sounds higher.

90912.q: What happens to the note when you make a string shorter with your finger?
90912.e: If you press the string onto the fingerboard, only a shorter part vibrates. The shorter part sounds higher.

90913.q: Which large instrument with very many strings do you pluck with both hands?
90913.e: The harp has a large frame with many strings. You pluck them with the fingers of both hands.
90913.m: The harp has very many strings.

90914.q: On which instrument of Swiss folk music do you strike strings with small hammers?
90914.e: On the Hackbrett, many strings lie across a flat wooden box. You strike them with small hammers. It is especially well known in the Appenzell region.
90914.m: On the Hackbrett you strike strings.

90915.q: What are the strings of instruments often made of today?
90915.e: Today strings are often made of steel or of the plastic nylon. They last well and sound good.
90915.m: Strings today are made of metal or plastic.

90916.q: What were many strings made of in the past?
90916.e: In the past, strings were made from dried and twisted sheep gut. They are called gut strings.
90916.m: In the past, strings were made of gut.

90917.q: Which of these instruments has strings?
90917.e: The zither is a flat box with many strings that you pluck. The other instruments have no strings.
90917.m: The zither is a string instrument.

90918.q: On which date was Sputnik 1 launched into orbit around the Earth?
90918.e: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 into space on 4 October 1957. This day is seen as the start of the space age.
90918.m: The space age began on 4 October 1957.

90919.q: What shape was the satellite Sputnik 1?
a: A ball with four long antennas
90919.e: Sputnik 1 was a shiny metal ball with four long rod antennas attached to it. It sent its radio signals through these antennas.
90919.m: Sputnik 1 was a metal ball with four antennas.

90920.q: Roughly what was the diameter of the Sputnik 1 ball?
90920.e: The Sputnik 1 ball had a diameter of about 58 centimetres. So it was roughly the size of a large exercise ball.
90920.m: Sputnik 1 was hardly bigger than an exercise ball.

90921.q: What did Sputnik 1 send to Earth that you could hear with a simple radio receiver?
90921.e: Sputnik 1 sent a simple “beep, beep” on radio frequencies. Radio amateurs all over the world could pick up the signal.
90921.m: The beeping of Sputnik 1 could be heard on the radio all over the world.

90922.q: Which rocket carried Sputnik 1 into space?
90922.e: Sputnik 1 was launched on a Soviet R-7. It had originally been built as the first intercontinental missile.
90922.m: The R-7 carried Sputnik 1 into orbit.

90923.q: What happened to Sputnik 1 in January 1958?
a: It burned up in the Earth’s atmosphere
It was taken to a museum
90923.e: The thin air slowly slowed Sputnik 1 down. After about three months it sank lower and burned up in the atmosphere in January 1958.
90923.m: Sputnik 1 burned up in the atmosphere after about three months.

90924.q: What does the Russian word “sputnik” mean in English?
90924.e: “Sputnik” means something like companion or fellow traveller. A satellite accompanies the Earth on its way.

90925.q: Which two countries competed in the space race during the Cold War?
a: The USA and the Soviet Union
90925.e: During the Cold War, the USA and the Soviet Union competed for success in space. Each side wanted to show its technical superiority.
90925.m: The space race was fought between the USA and the Soviet Union.

90926.q: What do you call the shock in the West caused by the launch of the first Soviet satellite in 1957?
90926.e: The USA was surprised that the Soviet Union was the first to put a satellite into space. This “Sputnik shock” led to large investments in research and education.
90926.m: The Sputnik shock pushed the USA to do more space research.

90927.q: Which country was the first to put a satellite into space in 1957?
90927.e: On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union launched the satellite Sputnik 1. It was the world’s first artificial satellite.
90927.m: The first satellite came from the Soviet Union.

90928.q: In which year was the US space agency NASA founded?
90928.e: NASA was founded in 1958 in response to Soviet successes in space. It later ran the Moon programme.

90929.q: What goal did US President John F. Kennedy announce in 1961?
a: To take people to the Moon before 1970
To build a station on Mars
To send a satellite around the Sun
To send the first dog into space
90929.e: In 1961 Kennedy called for a person to land on the Moon and be brought back safely before the end of the decade. The goal was reached in 1969.
90929.m: In 1961 Kennedy set the goal of a Moon landing by the end of the 1960s.

90930.q: Who was the first person to leave a spacecraft and float freely in space in 1965?
90930.e: The Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov left the spacecraft Voskhod 2 on 18 March 1965. He floated in space on a tether for about twelve minutes.
90930.m: Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk in 1965.

90931.q: Which country was the first to put people on the Moon?
90931.e: In 1969 the Americans Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon with Apollo 11. This meant the USA won this part of the race.
90931.m: In 1969 the USA put the first people on the Moon.

90932.q: Which joint space project of the USA and the Soviet Union is seen as the symbolic end of the space race?
90932.e: In 1975 an Apollo spacecraft and a Soyuz spacecraft docked with each other in space. The crews shook hands.
90932.m: In the Apollo-Soyuz project in 1975, the rivals worked together for the first time.

90933.q: On which day did Yuri Gagarin fly into space with Vostok 1?
90933.e: Yuri Gagarin was launched with Vostok 1 on 12 April 1961. He was the first person in space.
90933.m: The first person flew into space on 12 April 1961.

90934.q: Roughly how long did the flight of Vostok 1 last?
90934.e: Yuri Gagarin’s whole flight lasted about 108 minutes, so just under two hours. After that he was back on Earth.
90934.m: The flight of Vostok 1 lasted less than two hours.

90935.q: How many times did Vostok 1 orbit the Earth?
90935.e: Vostok 1 made exactly one orbit of the Earth. Then the spacecraft slowed down and came back into the atmosphere.
90935.m: Gagarin orbited the Earth just once.

90936.q: How did Yuri Gagarin reach the ground after his flight?
a: By parachute, separately from the capsule
Inside the capsule, landing on the sea
90936.e: A few kilometres above the ground, Gagarin was shot out of the capsule with the ejector seat. He landed with his own parachute, and the capsule landed separately.
90936.m: Gagarin landed by parachute near his capsule.

90937.q: Why did Yuri Gagarin wear a spacesuit inside the spacecraft?
a: For protection in case the capsule lost air
So that he would fly faster
So that he could be seen in the dark
Because it was the army uniform
90937.e: There is no air to breathe in space. The spacesuit would have protected Gagarin if the capsule had started to leak.
90937.m: A spacesuit protects you if there is no air in the capsule.

90938.q: What was Yuri Gagarin’s job before he became a cosmonaut?
90938.e: Yuri Gagarin was a pilot in the Soviet air force. The first cosmonauts were chosen mainly from young fighter pilots.
90938.m: Yuri Gagarin was a military pilot.

90939.q: Which day of remembrance is marked every year on 12 April?
a: International Day of Human Space Flight
90939.e: In 2011 the United Nations declared 12 April the International Day of Human Space Flight. It commemorates the flight of Vostok 1.
90939.m: On 12 April the Day of Human Space Flight is celebrated.

90940.q: Where did Yuri Gagarin land after his flight?
a: In a field in the Soviet Union
At an airport in the USA
90940.e: Gagarin landed by parachute in a field by the Volga, in what is now Russia. Farmers in the field were the first to see him.
90940.m: Gagarin landed in a field in the Soviet Union.

90941.q: What was the profession of Harrison Schmitt, the only scientist to walk on the Moon, in 1972?
90941.e: A geologist studies rocks. On Apollo 17, Harrison Schmitt examined the Moon rock right there on the spot.
90941.m: With Harrison Schmitt, a geologist stood on the Moon in 1972.

90942.q: How many crewed Moon landings were there in the Apollo programme?
90942.e: Apollo 11, 12, 14, 15, 16 and 17 landed on the Moon. Apollo 13 had to call off its landing.
90942.m: The Apollo programme achieved six Moon landings.

90943.q: Which rocket did the Apollo astronauts fly to the Moon on?
90943.e: The Saturn V was a huge three-stage rocket. It launched all the Moon missions.
90943.m: The Saturn V carried the Apollo spacecraft to the Moon.

90944.q: With which mission were people last on the Moon so far, in December 1972?
90944.e: Apollo 17 was the last Moon landing. Apollo 11 was the first, Apollo 13 had to turn back and Apollo 1 never took off.
90944.m: Apollo 17 in 1972 was the last Moon landing.

90945.q: What happened in 1967 during a test of the Apollo 1 capsule?
a: A fire killed the three astronauts
The rocket crashed into the sea
The capsule landed on the Moon
90945.e: During a test on the ground, a fire broke out in the capsule. The three astronauts Grissom, White and Chaffee were killed.
90945.m: Three astronauts died in the Apollo 1 fire in 1967.

90946.q: Which mission was the first to orbit the Moon with people on board, at Christmas 1968?
90946.e: Apollo 8 flew to the Moon in December 1968 and orbited it ten times. But the three astronauts did not land.
90946.m: In 1968 Apollo 8 took people into orbit around the Moon for the first time.

90947.q: What is the name of the famous photo from Apollo 8 that shows the Earth above the Moon’s horizon?
90947.e: The picture “Earthrise” shows the blue Earth above the grey surface of the Moon. It is seen as one of the most important photos of the 20th century.
90947.m: The photo “Earthrise” was taken on Apollo 8.

90948.q: Which vehicle did the astronauts of Apollo 15, 16 and 17 drive across the Moon?
a: A motorbike with a petrol engine
A tracked vehicle with a diesel engine
90948.e: The Moon buggy (the “Lunar Roving Vehicle”) ran on battery power. This let the astronauts cover much greater distances than on foot.
90948.m: On the last three Moon landings, the astronauts drove an electric Moon buggy.

90949.q: Which part of an Apollo spacecraft was the only one to return to Earth with the crew?
90949.e: The lunar module and the service module were separated along the way. Only the command module, with its heat shield, landed in the sea on parachutes.
90949.m: Only the command module brought the Apollo astronauts back.

90950.q: What was Apollo 13 actually supposed to do in 1970?
90950.e: Apollo 13 was meant to be the third Moon landing. Because of an explosion on board, the landing had to be cancelled.
90950.m: Apollo 13 was supposed to land on the Moon in 1970.

90951.q: What exploded on board Apollo 13 on the way to the Moon?
90951.e: A damaged oxygen tank in the service module exploded. As a result, power, water and breathing air in the main spacecraft largely failed.
90951.m: An oxygen tank exploded on Apollo 13.

90952.q: With which sentence did the crew of Apollo 13 report the breakdown to Earth?
90952.e: The crew radioed “Houston, we’ve had a problem”. The sentence later became world-famous.
90952.m: The famous radio message from Apollo 13 is “Houston, we’ve had a problem”.

90953.q: What did the crew of Apollo 13 use the lunar module for after the explosion?
a: As a store for Moon rock
90953.e: In the main spacecraft, power and breathing air had largely failed. So the three astronauts moved into the lunar module Aquarius until shortly before landing on Earth.
90953.m: On Apollo 13, the lunar module became a lifeboat.

90954.q: Which problem with the air did the Apollo 13 astronauts have to solve with tape and cardboard?
a: Too much carbon dioxide in the cabin
Too much oxygen in the cabin
Too much dust in the cabin
Too much humidity in the suits
90954.e: The lunar module’s filters were not enough for three people, and the square filters from the main spacecraft did not fit the round holders. With a home-made adapter, they removed the carbon dioxide.
90954.m: A home-made filter saved the Apollo 13 crew from too much carbon dioxide.

90955.q: How many astronauts flew on Apollo 13?
90955.e: On board were commander Jim Lovell, Jack Swigert and Fred Haise. All Apollo Moon flights had three people on board.
90955.m: Apollo 13 had three astronauts on board.

90956.q: Shortly before Apollo 13 was launched, an astronaut was replaced because he might have caught German measles. Why was that important?
a: He could have fallen ill in space, far from any help
Sick people are too heavy in weightlessness
You are not allowed to wear a spacesuit with German measles
90956.e: Ken Mattingly had been in contact with someone who had German measles. An illness on the way would have put the whole mission at risk, so Jack Swigert flew in his place. But Mattingly never fell ill.
90956.m: Illnesses in space can put a mission at risk.

90957.q: How did Apollo 13 get back to Earth after the breakdown?
a: It flew around the Moon and back
It turned around straight away in space
It landed briefly on the Moon
It waited for a rescue ship
90957.e: There was not enough power to turn straight back. With the help of gravity, Apollo 13 swung around the Moon and then flew back to Earth.
90957.m: Apollo 13 used the swing around the Moon for its journey home.

90958.q: In which year was the space probe Voyager 1 launched?
90958.e: Voyager 1 was launched in Florida in September 1977. The probe is still sending data today (as of 2026).

90959.q: Which two planets did Voyager 1 fly past?
90959.e: Voyager 1 reached Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980. After that it left the plane of the planets.

90960.q: Which moon of Saturn with a thick atmosphere did Voyager 1 study close up?
90960.e: The researchers steered Voyager 1 close past Titan. But the thick orange atmosphere hid the surface.
90960.m: Voyager 1 flew close past Saturn’s moon Titan.

90961.q: What does the photo “Pale Blue Dot”, taken by Voyager 1 in 1990, show?
a: The Earth as a tiny point of light
90961.e: Voyager 1 photographed the Earth from about 6 billion kilometres away. It appears only as a tiny bluish dot.
90961.m: In the photo “Pale Blue Dot”, the Earth is only a tiny dot.

90962.q: Why is the photo “Pale Blue Dot” by Voyager 1 so famous?
a: It shows how tiny the Earth is in space
It is the first photo of the Moon
It shows the inside of the Sun
90962.e: From about 6 billion kilometres away, the Earth is only a tiny point of light. The photo reminds many people how small and precious our planet is.
90962.m: The photo “Pale Blue Dot” shows how small the Earth is.

90963.q: Which region did Voyager 1 reach in 2012 as the first human-made object?
a: The centre of the Milky Way
